name: Glutathione
lead: Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. It is the most abundant low-molecular-weight thiol in most cell types and acts as an antioxidant, protecting cellular components from reactive oxygen species, peroxides and heavy metals, and it takes part in the detoxification of drugs and other xenobiotics [1].

For appearance, glutathione is used as a skin-lightening and skin-evening agent. People take it as capsules, sublingual or effervescent products, apply it in topical preparations, or receive it as an intravenous infusion or intradermal injection, in the hope of a lighter, more uniform complexion and less visible hyperpigmentation such as melasma or sun spots [5][13]. The proposed mechanisms include inhibition of tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production, a reduction in the oxidative stress that stimulates pigment cells, and a shift of melanin synthesis from dark eumelanin toward lighter pheomelanin [5][21]. The same use is discussed on looksmaxxing forums [3][4].

Human research consists of small, short randomized trials, open-label studies and several narrative and systematic reviews. A 2025 systematic review reported that several randomized trials of oral glutathione found a fall in skin melanin index compared with placebo, and that only one placebo-controlled study of intravenous glutathione had been published [5]. Intravenous use for lightening has drawn warnings from clinicians, dermatology authors and the government of the Philippines, as described below [13][14].

Outside cosmetics, glutathione and its precursors (such as N-acetylcysteine) are studied in many medical settings, and glutathione also appears in general wellness stacks and compounded injectable packages marketed by telehealth clinics [11].

angle.text: People use glutathione to lighten the overall skin tone or to even out dark patches such as melasma. Small randomized trials of oral and topical forms have reported lower instrument-measured melanin index than placebo, while the size and durability of visible change vary between studies.

paras: Glutathione is made in two ATP-dependent steps: glutamate-cysteine ligase joins glutamate and cysteine into gamma-glutamylcysteine (the rate-limiting step), and glutathione synthetase then adds glycine. Synthesis occurs in all animal cells, but liver synthesis is essential [1].

Inside healthy cells more than 90 percent of the pool is in the reduced form (GSH), the remainder being the disulfide form (GSSG), and the ratio of the two is used as a measure of cellular oxidative stress. Reduced glutathione is regenerated from GSSG by the enzyme glutathione reductase using NADPH [1]. Cellular concentrations are in the millimolar range, far higher than in extracellular fluid [1].

Beyond direct antioxidant roles, glutathione keeps vitamins C and E in their active forms, serves as a cysteine store, acts as a cofactor for glutathione peroxidases, and is conjugated to xenobiotics by glutathione S-transferases; the conjugation of the paracetamol (acetaminophen) metabolite NAPQI is a standard example. Paracetamol overdose depletes cellular glutathione, and N-acetylcysteine, a cysteine prodrug, is used to help restore it [1].

Wikipedia notes that the systemic availability of orally administered glutathione is described as poor, which is why research on oral products has focused on whether blood and tissue levels actually rise [1].

Wikipedia's article on skin whitening describes glutathione as the most common agent taken by mouth to lighten skin, and notes it is also used as a cream [13]. Products include capsules, sublingual and effervescent forms, dissolving oral films, topical lotions, soaps, and intravenous infusions or intradermal injections, sometimes combined with vitamin C or tranexamic acid [5][16][21].

Reviews describe the aims as general skin lightening, evening of tone and treatment of melasma and other hyperpigmentation [5][15]. Users on looksmaxxing forums discuss it chiefly for evening skin tone, lightening and fading marks, and some posters regard injectable forms as the strongest option [3][4].

Glutathione has been studied in a range of medical settings, for example intranasal glutathione in Parkinson's disease, oral glutathione in pediatric cystic fibrosis and glutathione in post-polio syndrome, each registered as a small clinical trial [24][25][26]. Supplement forums such as T Nation list it in general wellness stacks and among the compounded injectables offered by telehealth clinics [11].

Reviews describe three proposed mechanisms: inhibition of tyrosinase, the copper enzyme that begins melanin synthesis; reduction of the oxidative stress that stimulates melanogenesis; and a switch from dark eumelanin to lighter pheomelanin in the presence of thiols such as cysteine [5][21]. A 2026 narrative review notes that these are proposed mechanisms and that concurrent vitamin C use in some studies makes it harder to isolate the contribution of glutathione itself [21].

Whether swallowed glutathione reaches tissues has been debated, because peptidases in the gut and blood can break it down [1]. A 2015 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by Richie and colleagues in 54 non-smoking healthy adults gave 250 or 1,000 mg per day for six months. At six months, the higher-dose group showed roughly 30 to 35 percent increases in glutathione in red blood cells, plasma and lymphocytes and a larger rise in cheek cells, levels returned to baseline after a one-month washout, and markers of oxidative stress fell [6].

A 2022 clinical review by Sharma and Sharma argues that absorption through the lining of the mouth avoids digestion and may be higher, and discusses a dissolving film for that route, while noting that trials of glutathione for hyperpigmentation remain small and short and that no clinical guideline exists [16]. Researchers have also registered pharmacokinetic studies of newer micellar formulations [27].

Oral glutathione. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study by Arjinpathana and Asawanonda in Bangkok gave 60 healthy medical students 500 mg of glutathione daily or placebo for four weeks. Melanin indices fell at all six sites measured in the glutathione group, with differences from placebo reaching statistical significance at two sites, the right side of the face and the sun-exposed forearm. Both treatments were well tolerated, and the authors concluded that larger trials and long-term safety data were needed [7]. A 2009 registration lists a related trial of oral glutathione for skin whitening with 60 participants [8].

A three-arm 2017 trial in healthy women by Weschawalit and colleagues compared 250 mg per day of reduced glutathione, 250 mg per day of oxidized glutathione and placebo over 12 weeks. Melanin index and UV spots tended to be lower than with placebo for both forms, reduced glutathione was associated with fewer wrinkles at some sites, and no serious adverse effects were reported [17]. A 2016 open-label, single-arm study by Handog and colleagues gave a glutathione lozenge to 30 Filipino women with Fitzpatrick skin types IV or V for eight weeks, and melanin indices fell significantly from baseline, with changes visible from week two [18]. A 2022 randomized trial examined oral L-cystine combined with reduced glutathione against benchmark and placebo comparators [9].

Topical glutathione. A matched-pair, double-blind trial by Watanabe and colleagues in 30 healthy women aged 30 to 50 applied 2 percent oxidized glutathione lotion to one side of the face and placebo to the other, twice daily for 10 weeks. Melanin index was significantly lower on the glutathione side from early in the study, and later in the study that side also showed higher moisture, less wrinkle formation and better smoothness [19].

Intravenous glutathione. A 2016 review in the South African Medical Journal by Davids, Van Wyk and Khumalo searched the literature to September 2015 and reported that small trials and case series of oral, topical and soap-based glutathione described lighter skin, that studies of intravenous glutathione lasted from a few doses to 4 to 12 weeks with mostly few side effects reported, and that no studies of long-term intravenous use or its safety for lightening had been published; they called for regulatory review [14]. A 2020 evidence-based review by Sitohang and Ninditya examined three randomized trials of systemic glutathione in adults and reported that one found no whitening effect and the other two found effects in limited body areas or age groups; it described oral glutathione as well tolerated and noted that the effects did not last [15].

Systematic and narrative reviews. A 2025 systematic review in the International Journal of Dermatology by Sarkar and colleagues searched PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library over ten years. It reported that 0.5 percent topical glutathione outperformed 0.1 percent and placebo, that five randomized trials and one open-label study of oral glutathione found a significantly lower melanin index than placebo, that combined topical 2 percent and oral glutathione outperformed either alone, and that benefits of topical and oral forms were not sustained. It found one placebo-controlled study of intravenous glutathione and concluded intravenous use was contraindicated because of lack of efficacy and side effects [5]. A 2026 narrative review by Aloraini and colleagues reported modest, variable pigmentation improvements across studies that were generally small, methodologically inconsistent and short [21]. A scoping review of systemic glutathione for skin lightening by Dlova and colleagues appeared in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology in 2026 [22].

A systematic review of antioxidants in melasma, covering vitamin C, cysteamine, silymarin and other agents, is listed alongside these; the findings in its abstract concern agents other than glutathione [10]. In all, outcomes in the lightening trials are mostly instrumental (melanin index) and the studies vary in dose, product, duration and population.

Wikipedia reports that the government of the Philippines recommends against intravenous glutathione for skin lightening because of possible side effects [13]. Reviews by Davids and colleagues (2016) and by Sarkar and colleagues (2025) describe a lack of long-term safety data for intravenous use, and the 2026 narrative review lists reported concerns including liver toxicity, hypersensitivity and possible renal and endocrine effects [14][5][21]. A 2017 letter in the Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association discusses intravenous glutathione for fair skin and its adverse effects [23].

A 2025 case report in Cureus described a previously healthy woman who developed a systemic inflammatory response, high fever, shock and acute liver injury within an hour of an unregulated high-dose glutathione infusion sold for skin lightening; she recovered with supportive care. The authors suggested endotoxin contamination or an interaction with high-dose glutathione and very low food intake, and called for stronger regulation of cosmetic intravenous therapies [20].

Oral and topical products in the trials above were generally described as well tolerated over weeks to months, and the 2015 body-store trial reported no safety problems over six months, though the authors of the lightening trials note that long-term safety has not been established [7][6][17][19]. Oral glutathione supplements are sold in many countries as dietary supplements. Homeopathic products listing glutathione appear in the US DailyMed database, with labels stating that their indications have not been reviewed by the FDA [12].

Skin-lightening products have a long commercial history in South and Southeast Asia, Africa and diasporic communities, and glutathione products are marketed in several of these markets [13]. A 2026 review describes intravenous glutathione as a popular cosmetic skin-lightening treatment [21].

On looksmaxxing forums, threads present glutathione as a way to obtain a lighter or more even complexion and share experiences with oral and injectable forms [3][4]. Posters on T Nation more often mention glutathione as part of clinic-supplied injectable packages or general supplementation; one poster listed it with testosterone, hCG and peptides in a monthly clinic bill [11].

timeline.event: A trial of oral glutathione for skin whitening (60 participants) is registered [8].
Arjinpathana and Asawanonda publish a four-week randomized placebo-controlled study of 500 mg daily oral glutathione in 60 students [7].
Watanabe and colleagues report a 10-week split-face trial of 2 percent topical oxidized glutathione [19].
Richie and colleagues publish a six-month randomized trial of oral glutathione and body glutathione stores in 54 adults [6].
Handog and colleagues report an open-label lozenge study in Filipino women; Davids and colleagues publish a review of intravenous glutathione safety data [18][14].
Weschawalit and colleagues publish a 12-week three-arm trial of reduced and oxidized glutathione [17].
Sitohang and Ninditya publish an evidence-based review of systemic glutathione as a whitening agent [15].
Clinical review of oral mucosal glutathione absorption and pigmentation published [16].
Sarkar and colleagues publish a systematic review of glutathione in lightening and melasma; a case report describes severe reaction to a high-dose cosmetic infusion [5][20].
Narrative and scoping reviews of intravenous, oral and topical glutathione for lightening are published [21][22].

lore.intro: Glutathione appears in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums mainly as a skin-lightening agent and as a general antioxidant supplement, often alongside other injectables [3][4][11].

claims.believers: Forum posters describe glutathione as a route to a lighter, more even complexion and report visible change after weeks of use [3].
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review found that several small randomized trials showed reduced melanin index with oral glutathione versus placebo, and that topical and oral benefits were not sustained; the studies varied in dose and design [5].

claims.claim: Injectable glutathione is the 'real deal' and works better than pills
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread presents injectable glutathione as the more effective form for lightening [4].
claims.experts: The 2025 review found one placebo-controlled study of intravenous glutathione [5]; the Philippine government advises against intravenous use for lightening [13], and a 2025 case report describes a severe reaction after an unregulated infusion [20].

claims.claim: Oral glutathione is destroyed in the gut and does nothing
claims.believers: Some posters argue that swallowed glutathione is broken down before reaching skin, so oral products are pointless; others report results regardless [3].
claims.experts: A six-month placebo-controlled trial found raised glutathione in blood cells and cheek cells with oral dosing [6], and several trials report melanin-index changes [5]; reviews also describe oral bioavailability as a debated point [1][16].

claims.claim: Taking glutathione with NAC or vitamin C boosts lightening
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether combining glutathione and NAC helps with lightening and tan removal [28].
claims.experts: NAC is a cysteine precursor used to help restore glutathione in paracetamol overdose [1]; the 2026 review notes that concurrent vitamin C in some studies makes it difficult to isolate glutathione's effect [21]. No trial cited here tests glutathione plus NAC for tone.

claims.claim: Glutathione works as a general detox and health booster for lifters
claims.believers: T Nation posters list glutathione in supplement stacks or cite it as important to detoxification and illness recovery [11].
claims.experts: Glutathione is central to cellular redox and xenobiotic metabolism [1], and the 2015 trial reported lower oxidative-stress markers with supplementation [6]; effects of supplementing on appearance or training outcomes in healthy adults have not been tested in the studies cited here.
